analysis: Catalogued as two rare 16th-century German battle maps. They are 17th century, and the sheets say so. The left plate is titled 'Abriss der Schlacht so zwischen Herren Marggrafen von Durlach und Monsieur Tylli als Kays. und Bayrischen Generalen vorgangen' -- the Battle of Wimpfen, 6 May 1622, Margrave Georg Friedrich of Baden-Durlach against Tilly, in the Thirty Years' War. The right plate is a bird's-eye view of the same engagement on the Neckar with the armies drawn up in blocks and the powder-magazine explosion that decided it. Both are copperplate engravings in the Matthaeus Merian manner and are almost certainly from the Theatrum Europaeum or a contemporary relation, so c.1633-1650. That makes them roughly 375 years old, the oldest printed matter in this section, and $400-600 for two framed Merian-school plates is at or below the market.
problems: The catalogue's date is wrong by a century, which cuts both ways -- it will suppress specialist interest, and it means the description cannot be relied on for anything else either. Both sheets are toned and the right one has visible edge damage and losses at the lower margin where the letterpress key runs, with the frame's backing paper failing. Merian plates were reprinted from the original copperplates into the 18th century and facsimiled in the 19th; the platemark and paper need checking out of the frame. The right plate's title and key are partly trimmed or obscured.
patience: Moderate. Merian plates run regularly in map and book sales; a matched pair of Wimpfen views is a less common offering.

analysis: A small engraved powder horn with the full British royal arms -- crown, lion and unicorn supporters, the quartered shield, and the Garter motto HONI SOIT QUI MAL Y PENSE running round the belt. The horn has a genuine deep amber patination with the engraved lines darkened by age and handling rather than by fresh ink, and the turned spout with its incised rings is period work. Third of a three-horn consignment (2166, 2167, 2168) and by far the cheapest, at $300-500 -- inside the band with room, which the other two are not.
problems: The house's own grading is the honest guide here: the Fort Ticonderoga horn at 2166 is dated, named and placed and carries $10,000-15,000; this one has no name, no place and no date, only heraldry, and is priced accordingly. Engraved powder horns are also among the most faked objects in American arms collecting, and the fakes are made on genuine old horns, which defeats the obvious test -- judge the engraving, not the horn: period cutting is confident and slightly irregular with age-darkened lines, modern work is too even and the lines stay pale. The openwork finial at the spout looks like a later addition rather than an original stopper. 'Rev War' in the title is an inference from the arms, not evidence.
patience: Moderate to low. Engraved 18th-century horns are genuinely scarce; undated armorial ones are the affordable end of a scarce thing.

analysis: Two early Bible leaves, $300-400. Single leaves from incunable and early printed Bibles -- and from manuscript ones -- are the cheapest way into genuinely old printed matter, precisely because they are broken out of books that were already imperfect. A leaf from a 15th- or 16th-century Bible costs less than a modern print and is four to five centuries older than anything else on the wall. This satisfies the age criterion outright and inside the band.
problems: 'Early' is not a date and 'Bible leaves' is not an edition. The range runs from a 15th-century manuscript vellum leaf (several hundred dollars) through a Nuremberg or Koberger incunable leaf (similar) to a 19th-century facsimile (nothing). Identify the edition at preview: the type, the rubrication, the paper or vellum and the watermark all speak. Leaf-breaking also means these have no completeness value and never will.
patience: High. Bible leaves are a steady trade and available online at any time -- which is itself a reason not to stretch.

analysis: Eight early New Hampshire documents from a display, $300-400 -- roughly $40-50 a document for New England manuscript material. Early American documents are one of the few genuinely antique categories where the budget buys real things rather than fragments, and New Hampshire is close enough to be regionally interesting to a midcoast collector without being priced as Maine material.
problems: 'Early' with no date range, and the value of manuscript documents depends entirely on who signed them and what they concern -- a routine 1790s deed is $30, a document signed by a provincial governor or a Revolutionary officer is many times that. 'From a display' means they have been mounted, and mounting usually means hinges, adhesive and light exposure. Read all eight at preview; the lot is worth what its best document is worth.
patience: Moderate. Early New England document groups run periodically.

analysis: An early vellum diploma, $100-200 -- the cheapest lot in the books section and one that almost certainly clears the antique line. European university and guild diplomas on vellum, with wax seals and engrossed calligraphy, are handsome documents and were produced from the 16th century onward.
problems: 'Early' again does no work; no university, no date, no country. Vellum cockles and the ink can flake; wax seals crack and are often missing entirely, and the seal is much of the visual appeal. Latin engrossing hands are difficult to read, so budget for not knowing exactly what you own.

analysis: German masters' and doctoral diplomas of 1739, in a case with a seal, $300-500. Dated to the year in the catalogue, so the age evidence is Catalogued rather than inferred, and 1739 puts this among the oldest dated objects in the sale. Diplomas surviving in their original round document case with the seal intact are considerably better than loose ones -- the case is usually the first thing lost.
problems: No university named and no graduate named, both of which affect value. Confirm the case and seal actually belong to these documents rather than having been associated later. Vellum or heavy paper of this date is usually cockled and the wax seal chipped. At $396-660 all-in it is comfortably in band, so the risk is small.
patience: Moderate. Cased 18th-century diplomas with seals are an irregular offering.

analysis: John Strype on the Archbishops of Canterbury, 1718, $300-400 -- one of a pair of Strype volumes in the sale (see 2330, dated 1711). Strype's ecclesiastical biographies are foundational English historical scholarship and genuine early-18th-century folios. Three hundred years old, in band, and the date is catalogued.
problems: Strype's works are not scarce -- they were printed in decent numbers and have been reprinted since -- and the market for 18th-century English ecclesiastical history is thin. Value turns on binding condition, completeness of plates and whether the volume is a first or a later edition, none of which is stated. Expect a rebacked or worn contemporary calf binding, which is normal and not fatal.
patience: High. Strype volumes appear in most antiquarian book sales.

analysis: John Strype, Archbishops of Canterbury, 1711, $300-400 -- companion to 2327 and seven years earlier. Same reasoning: genuinely antique, catalogued to the year, in band.
problems: Same as 2327. Two Strype lots in one sale means they compete with each other -- watch which one runs first and bid the second.

analysis: Still a genuinely antique complete five-volume set of Mme de Montolieu's 'Le Robinson Suisse', with twelve illustrations and a map of the island, in full calf with applied gilt labels. But the description changes both the date and the condition. It gives the imprint as 'Paris, Chez Arthus Bertrand, 1826' where the lot title says 1824 -- one of the two is wrong, and it matters for an edition-sensitive book.
problems: The bindings are failing, which I had asked about and assumed the best of: 'BOARDS OFF OR LOOSE, but present, LEATHER SPINE COVERING HALF GONE ON VOL 2; off but present from vol 4, scattered edge...'. That is a set needing rebacking on at least two volumes to be shelvable, which costs more than the lot. Complete and present, but not sound. Downgraded from BUY on that basis. Also reconcile the 1824 in the title against the 1826 in the description before bidding.

analysis: A Siege of Yorktown map by Stedman, $300-400. Charles Stedman's 'History of the Origin, Progress, and Termination of the American War' was published in London in 1794 with a series of engraved battle plans, and the Yorktown plan is among the most sought of them -- it is the decisive engagement of the Revolution mapped by a British officer who was there. Genuinely 18th century, genuinely in band, and Revolutionary cartography is a durable market.
problems: Stedman plans are usually sold as extracted plates, so expect a sheet with fold lines and possible offsetting from the facing text. Check for trimming into the platemark and for a later hand-colouring, which on Revolutionary maps is common and reduces value to purists. The date is inferred from the publication rather than stated.
patience: Moderate. Stedman plans appear regularly in map sales but Yorktown is the one people want.

analysis: A framed 1846 book prospectus, 'Origin of Steam Navigation', $200-300. Dated to the year, genuinely antique, and a printed prospectus is an unusual survival -- these were throwaway advertising and almost none was kept. The steam-navigation subject also connects to the marine material.
problems: A prospectus is ephemera: interesting, cheap, and with a shallow resale market. Framed, so the verso and any subscriber annotations are hidden, and 1846 paper behind glass for decades will have light-struck and acidified. Estimate is at the top of what printed ephemera makes.

analysis: A three-volume set on Rabelais, described as rare, $200-300. Rabelais scholarship and illustrated editions span four centuries, and a three-volume set at $65-100 a volume is cheap for anything early.
problems: No date, no edition, no language, no illustrator -- 'rare' is doing all the work and the standing scepticism about auction copywriting applies. A Dore-illustrated 19th-century Rabelais is common; a 17th-century one is not; nothing here says which. Rabelais editions are also frequently incomplete or made up.

analysis: Five volumes of French Salon yearbooks, 1889-1893, $500-700. Dated to the year, genuinely antique, and the Salon catalogues with their photogravure plates are a useful reference as well as an object -- they document exactly what was hanging in Paris in those years, which is how you check a period attribution.
problems: Estimate is at the top of the band ($660-924 all-in) for reference books with a limited resale market. Large, heavy folios; expect broken hinges and loose plates, which is what always happens to these. Confirm the plates are present -- Salon volumes are routinely broken for their photogravures.

analysis: Twenty-nine volumes of Shakespeare plus two Yale Shakespeare, $200-300 -- about $7 a volume, which is honest box-lot pricing for a decorative set.
problems: No date and no edition. The Yale Shakespeare began in 1918, so at least part of this straddles the antique line. Multi-volume Shakespeare sets are the classic decorator's-shelf purchase and have almost no resale value; thirty-one volumes is four feet of shelf. Buy for the look, not as a book purchase.

analysis: A box lot that turns out to be dated. The description lists '(4 vol set) "Le Cabinet de l'Amateur et de l'Antiquaire", Paris au Bureau du Journal, 1842-1846, orig half leather spine, PLUS (2 vols) "The Genuine Works of Flavius Josephus" by the Late Wm. Whiston, MA, J. Grigg, Philadelphia, 1829, orig...'. So at least six of the fourteen volumes are firmly pre-1850, in original bindings, and one is a complete four-volume run of a French connoisseurship journal. At $300-400 for fourteen volumes that is roughly $25 each for genuinely antique books. I had this as an unassessable box lot; it is not.
problems: Still a box lot, and the remaining eight volumes are unlisted -- assume they are the makeweight. Early-19th-century half leather almost always has cracked joints and detached boards; 'orig half leather spine' is a description, not a condition report. The Josephus is a common American edition and the French journal has a narrow audience. Read the spines at preview.
patience: Moderate. Mixed antiquarian box lots run constantly, but ones with a complete dated set inside are the minority.

analysis: Five complete volumes of 'Masterpieces of French Art', $500-700. Turn-of-the-century subscription art folios were produced in enormous quantities, are physically imposing and are worth very little -- the plates are the only part anyone wants and they are usually broken out.
problems: Estimate is well above the market. No date. Large folios with the usual broken hinges. Subscription art sets are the most oversupplied category in the antiquarian book trade.

analysis: Eight 'early' medium-format children's picture books, $250-350. Early illustrated children's books can be genuinely valuable -- Rackham, Dulac, Potter, Greenaway -- but only if the illustrator and edition are named, and none is.
problems: No titles, no illustrators, no dates. 'Early' is unusable. Children's books also suffer the worst condition of any category because children owned them; expect crayon, tears and missing plates. Estimate assumes named illustrators the catalogue does not claim.

analysis: A 1912 book on elephant hunting, first edition, first issue, $600-800. Dated, genuinely antique, and the big-game hunting literature of the Edwardian period -- Selous, Bell, Stigand -- is a real collecting field with committed buyers. But no author or title is given, which for a first-edition-first-issue claim is a remarkable omission: the issue point is the whole basis of the description.
problems: Above the comfortable band at $792-1,056 all-in. An unnamed first edition cannot be checked. Africana hunting literature is also a field where condition, the dust jacket and the specific issue drive tenfold differences. And this is a book about shooting elephants, which is a subject decision as much as a collecting one.

analysis: Twenty-eight volumes of the signed Rudyard Kipling Burwash Edition with dust jackets, $3,000-4,000. The Burwash was Doubleday's American limited edition of 1937-39, and a complete signed set with jackets is a genuine rarity -- Kipling died in January 1936, so the 'signed' element needs careful checking. Four to five times the band.
problems: Above budget at $3,960-5,280 all-in. Kipling died in 1936 and the Burwash Edition was published 1937-39, so the signature is presumably on tipped-in leaves signed earlier or is a facsimile -- establish which, because it is the difference between a $4,000 set and a $600 one. Twenty-eight volumes with jackets means twenty-eight jackets to assess.
patience: Low. Complete signed Burwash sets with jackets are genuinely scarce.

analysis: A signed first edition of Esther Forbes's 'Johnny Tremain', 1943 Newbery winner, $500-1,000. A genuinely desirable modern first -- signed Newbery firsts in jacket are a real market and the estimate spans it honestly. Post-1926, so no age criterion, and at $660-1,320 all-in it straddles the top of the band.
problems: Straddles the budget ceiling. The value is entirely in the jacket and the signature, and neither is described: a first in a fine jacket is several times a first without one. 'Signed' needs to mean signed by Forbes rather than by a later owner. Also worth knowing: Forbes was a Massachusetts writer and this is a New England book, but that is the only connection to the collection.

analysis: Anson's 'A Voyage Round the World', first edition 1747, with the subscriber's list, $1,000-1,500. This is one of the genuinely important books in the sale -- the account of Anson's circumnavigation of 1740-44 was the bestselling voyage narrative of the 18th century and the first edition with the subscriber's list is the one collectors want. It hits the age criterion by nearly three centuries and the marine interest squarely. It is also $1,320-1,980 all-in, above the band.
problems: Above budget. First-edition Anson is common enough that condition and completeness decide the price: it should have 42 folding plates and charts, and extracted or supplied plates are routine. Check the plate count and the binding. 'First edition' of Anson is itself complicated -- several 1748 issues followed within months.
patience: Moderate. Anson firsts appear in most voyage-and-travel sales.

analysis: A group of early 19th-century letters from the sea captain Roberts family of Manchester, Vermont, $500-700. Manuscript sea-captain correspondence is exactly the intersection of the antique and marine criteria, and family letter groups are where the real texture of the coasting and deep-water trades survives. Catalogued to the period.
problems: At $660-924 all-in it is at the top of the band. Manuscript letter groups are worth what their contents are worth, and that means reading them -- a group of routine family news is $150, a group describing voyages, cargoes and ports is several times that. Manchester, Vermont is an odd home port for a sea captain and worth reconciling. Iron-gall ink burns through paper over time; check for losses at the folds.

analysis: A group of War of 1812 Royal Navy documents, some signed by admirals, $2,000-3,000. Genuinely antique, genuinely marine, and admiral-signed naval documents from the 1812 war are a real and well-supported market on both sides of the Atlantic. Three to four times the band at $2,640-3,960 all-in.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin. 'Some admirals signed' does not say which admirals, and that is the entire valuation -- a Cochrane or a Warren signature is worth many times a routine dockyard signature. Naval autograph material is also forged.

analysis: Herman Moll's 'Beaver Map' of British North America, c.1730, $6,000-8,000. This is the most important single sheet in the sale: Moll's 'A New and Exact Map of the Dominions of the King of Great Britain on ye Continent of North America', with its inset of beavers at Niagara, is one of the landmark maps of colonial America. The estimate is in the market. It is six to eight times the band.
problems: Massively above budget. Moll's Beaver Map went through numerous states between 1715 and the 1750s and the state materially affects value; 'ca 1730' is a broad claim. Large folding maps are usually backed, and backing halves the price. Not reachable here.
patience: Low. A genuinely scarce and important map.

analysis: Greenleaf's 1843 State of Maine schoolhouse map, the first with the final border, $6,000-8,000. For a Maine collector this is the single most desirable object in the sale on subject alone -- Moses Greenleaf's maps are the foundational cartography of the state, and the 1843 issue is the first to show the boundary as settled by the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842. Genuinely antique, hyper-local, historically pointed. And six to eight times the band.
problems: Massively above budget at $7,920-10,560 all-in. Schoolhouse wall maps of this date are almost always on linen with rollers and are almost always damaged -- varnish darkening, splits along the folds, losses at the edges. At this estimate condition needs to be exceptional and nothing here describes it.
patience: Low. Greenleaf wall maps are scarce and this is the wanted issue -- a genuine regret, not a pass on merit.

analysis: 'The Designs of Inigo Jones', published by William Kent, 1727, volume I only, $1,200-1,500. A foundational English architectural folio and a genuinely important 18th-century book. Above the band at $1,584-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget, and volume I only -- the work was published in two volumes and a broken set is worth substantially less than half. Large folios of this date are usually rebound or rebacked and the plates are frequently extracted. Check the plate count against the collation.

analysis: Twenty-two letters from US senators, representatives and others, 1939-1946, including one from JFK in May 1958. The dates in the title contradict each other -- a 1958 letter is not within 1939-1946 -- which is worth flagging. Political autograph material with a JFK letter has a real market and the estimate reflects it. Post-1926 throughout, and above the band at $1,320-2,640 all-in.
problems: Above budget. The internal date contradiction in the catalogue title suggests the lot was assembled hastily. JFK signatures are among the most Autopen-signed and most forged in American political autographs, and a 1958 letter -- when he was a sitting senator with a heavy correspondence -- is squarely in Autopen territory. Authentication is essential and none is offered.

analysis: Two 19th-century autograph letters, $500-700. Catalogued to the century, so antique, and manuscript letters are a category where the budget genuinely buys the real thing.
problems: Neither correspondent is named, which is the only thing that matters in autograph material -- two letters by unremarkable people are worth $40, two by a known hand are worth many multiples. At $660-924 all-in the estimate assumes names the catalogue does not supply. Read them at preview.

analysis: A rare 18th-century estate map of Kent, UK, $1,000-1,500. Manuscript estate maps are genuine one-off documents -- surveyed and drawn by hand for a specific landowner -- and that makes them unique rather than editioned, which is a real distinction. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget. English estate maps have a narrow market and it is in England, not New England. No estate, parish or surveyor named. Large manuscript maps on paper or vellum are usually folded, split at the folds and stained.

analysis: An 1807 Royal Academy letter signed by David as Secretary, $1,000-1,500. Dated, antique, and an institutional autograph with a documented office. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget. 'David' is doing a lot of work here: the Royal Academy's Secretary in 1807 was not Jacques-Louis David, who was French, in Paris and not a Royal Academician -- if the lot is being presented to imply otherwise, that is the trap. Establish exactly which David signed and in what capacity before treating this as a name lot.

analysis: A 1768 Book of Common Prayer signed by Sir John Thorold in 1772, $600-800. Dated to the year with a dated ownership signature four years later -- that is unusually good documentation for a book at this level, and a named baronet's ownership inscription is real provenance rather than the boilerplate the standing brief warns about. Genuinely antique by 258 years.
problems: At $792-1,056 all-in it sits at the very top of the band. Eighteenth-century prayer books are not scarce; the Thorold association is what lifts this, and Thorold is a Lincolnshire baronetcy of modest fame. Check the binding is contemporary and that the inscription is period ink rather than a later addition -- provenance inscriptions are the easiest thing in the book world to fake.

analysis: Three French folios, $250-350. Priced as a box lot, which is the right way to sell three unidentified books, and folio format usually means something with plates.
problems: No titles, no dates, no subjects. 'French folios' is a description of the binding size and the language. Large French folios are also the hardest books to resell in America. Preview lot.

analysis: Two Islamic manuscript Qur'an leaves, $500-700. Manuscript leaves in Arabic script with illumination are genuinely hand-written documents and, like the Bible leaves at 1487, are an affordable way to own something several centuries old.
problems: No date, no region, no script identified -- Maghribi, Naskh, Muhaqqaq and Kufic all price differently and all date differently. Qur'an leaves are also produced as modern souvenirs on artificially aged paper in some markets. And there is a handling consideration worth stating plainly: these are leaves from a sacred text that were broken out of a complete manuscript, which some buyers will not want to participate in. At $660-924 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band for something undated.

analysis: A Persian manuscript miniature with calligraphy, $200-400 -- the cheaper of the two Islamic manuscript lots and the more decorative. Persian miniatures with facing calligraphy are attractive objects and the format is a genuine tradition.
problems: Persian miniatures are the single most reproduced category of Islamic art: modern Isfahan workshops produce them in quantity on old paper, sometimes on genuinely old blank leaves taken from period manuscripts, which defeats paper-dating. No date, no school, no subject named. Judge on pigment quality, gold application and the confidence of the line.

analysis: A 1930 art press book illustrated by Marie Laurencin (1885-1956), $1,000-2,000. Laurencin is a documented and collected artist and livres d'artiste of this date with her lithographs are a real market. Dated to the year and firmly post-1926. Above the band at $1,320-2,640 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Livre d'artiste value depends on the edition size, the number and state of the plates, whether the copy is signed and whether it is one of the deluxe issues -- none of which is given. No title, no press, no author.

analysis: A Chinese export pewter tea caddy with tea leaves still in it, $250-350 -- not a book at all, it lands here on the word 'caddy'. Chinese export pewter tea caddies were shipped with the tea trade through the 19th century and are honest, useful objects. The surviving tea is a small charming detail.
problems: Pewter is soft and dents, and export caddies are frequently missing their inner lids. No date. Pewter has no melt floor worth calculating -- the metal is worth pennies. Export pewter is also reproduced.

analysis: A Victorian faux book-form tea caddy, $600-800. A genuine Victorian conceit -- a caddy disguised as a bound volume, sometimes as a stack of them -- and a well-made one in tooled leather with a working lock is an appealing object with real period charm.
problems: At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band. Book-form caddies are reproduced heavily for the decorator trade and modern ones are convincing at photograph distance; the tells are the interior (a period one is lead- or foil-lined with tea staining) and the leather tooling. Interior fittings and the lid are almost always missing or replaced.

analysis: A Victorian black walnut two-part secretary bookcase, $1,000-1,500 -- furniture, filed here by the word 'bookcase'. Genuinely antique, but this is the heart of the weak market the standing brief names: large Victorian case furniture has fallen further than any other antique category and shows no sign of returning.
problems: Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in for a category where the same piece will be worth less in ten years. Two-part case furniture is also a moving and siting problem -- these are seven feet tall and very heavy.
patience: Very high. Victorian secretaries are in every sale and frequently pass unsold.

analysis: A Springfield Model 1873 trapdoor rifle in .45-70, $600-800. This is the standard US Army rifle of the Indian Wars period and a genuine 19th-century American military arm -- it satisfies the age criterion outright. It is also, being manufactured before 1899, an 'antique firearm' under federal law rather than a 'firearm', which in principle means no FFL transfer is required; that materially changes what buying it involves compared with the modern guns in this consignment. Verify the serial-number date and confirm Maine's own position before relying on it.
problems: Trapdoors were made in enormous numbers over twenty years and value swings on the model year, the serial range, matching parts and bore condition, none of which is given. Many surviving trapdoors are parts guns assembled from several rifles, and cut-down or 'sporterized' examples are common. Check the stock cartouches, the breech-block model marking and whether the rear sight is correct for the serial. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band.
patience: Moderate. Trapdoors run regularly in arms sales; honest all-matching ones are the smaller share.

analysis: A Jackie Brown percussion long rifle in .45, $700-900. A percussion muzzleloader is pre-cartridge technology and, as a muzzle-loading arm, sits outside the federal firearm definition entirely regardless of date -- the simplest thing to buy in the whole arms consignment. Whether it is a 19th-century original or a modern reproduction is the question the name is supposed to answer.
problems: 'Jackie Brown' does not resolve to a documented 19th-century American gunsmith and reads much more like a modern contemporary-longrifle maker -- there is a substantial and skilled community building period-correct flintlock and percussion rifles today, and their work is signed. If that is what this is, it is a well-made modern rifle worth roughly the estimate and not an antique at all. Establish the maker before treating the age claim as real. At $924-1,188 all-in it is above the band as estimated.

analysis: A Gillespie derringer in .38, $500-700. Percussion and early-cartridge pocket pistols of the mid-19th century are genuine antiques and, if pre-1899, are antique firearms under federal law rather than firearms. Small, displayable, and inside the band.
problems: 'Gillespie' is an uncommon maker name and needs verifying -- there were Gillespie gunsmiths in North Carolina making longrifles, which is a different thing entirely from a derringer. Derringers are also the most faked of all American handguns because they are small and the good names (Deringer of Philadelphia especially) carry a premium. Confirm the barrel markings and the lock. Calibre given as .38 suggests cartridge rather than percussion, which affects the pre-1899 question.

analysis: A Marlin Model 1893 saddle ring carbine in .32-40, $600-800. Saddle ring carbines are the desirable configuration of the 1893 and .32-40 is a scarcer chambering than the common .30-30. If the serial dates it before 1899 it is an antique firearm federally, which simplifies acquisition considerably.
problems: The Model 1893 ran from 1893 to 1936, so most surviving examples are post-1899 and are ordinary modern firearms for transfer purposes -- the serial number decides it and is not given. Saddle rings are also added to plain carbines to increase value, and carbines are made up from rifles by shortening barrels. Bore condition on a .32-40 matters and is not described. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band.

analysis: A Marlin Model 1894 lever action rifle in .32-20, $1,000-1,500. Companion to the 1893 carbine at 1236 and the same reasoning, one model year later. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Model 1894 production ran from 1894 to 1935, so 'antique' status depends entirely on a serial number that is not given. No condition or bore information.

analysis: A Nagant M1895 revolver in 7.62x38mmR, $300-500. The gas-seal Nagant is a genuinely unusual mechanism -- the cylinder moves forward to seal against the barrel -- and they are cheap because Russia and the Soviet Union made them by the million into the 1940s. An interesting object, not an investment.
problems: Although the model dates from 1895, the overwhelming majority of surviving Nagants are Soviet-era production and therefore ordinary modern firearms requiring an FFL transfer, with the acquisition friction and cost that implies for an out-of-state online buyer. Import marks, refinishing and mismatched numbers are the norm. Ammunition is scarce and expensive.
patience: Very high. Nagants are among the most available surplus handguns there are.

analysis: A Henry Atkin (From Purdey's) side-by-side 12-bore, $1,500-2,000. Atkin was a genuine London best-gun maker and 'From Purdey's' is his authentic trading style, marking him as a Purdey-trained gunmaker who set up on his own in 1877. A real London gun. Above the band at $1,980-2,640 all-in.
problems: Above budget. English best guns of this age need proof, barrel-wall thickness and chamber-length measurement before they can be shot, and re-proofing an out-of-proof gun costs real money. No date, no serial, no barrel-length or condition information. Also note that this is the modest end of a five-lot fine-gun consignment (1234, 1238, 1240, 1249, 1253) that runs to a $100,000-150,000 Purdey pair.

analysis: A matched pair of Purdey shotguns in their case, 12-bore, $100,000-150,000 -- by an order of magnitude the highest-estimated lot in the entire sale, and roughly a hundred and fifty times the budget band. A cased matched Purdey pair is the pinnacle of English gunmaking and the estimate is a real one.
problems: Entirely out of reach. Noted here only because a lot at this level tells you something about the sale: a house handling a six-figure Purdey pair is also the house cataloguing 'Lille 1737' on an 1880s platter, and that inconsistency is worth carrying into every other lot.

analysis: A Battista Rizzini S782 EMEL over-under 20-bore, $10,000-15,000. A modern Italian best-quality sidelock, contemporary production, ten to fifteen times the band.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin. Modern firearm requiring FFL transfer. No criteria fit whatever.

analysis: A Simson & Co. shotgun made for Iver Johnson, 12-bore, $2,000-2,500. Simson of Suhl was a serious German maker and the Iver Johnson contract guns are a documented curiosity. Post-1926 in all likelihood and three times the band.
problems: Above budget. Modern firearm for transfer purposes unless pre-1899, which Simson-Iver Johnson contract guns are not. Damascus versus fluid-steel barrels is the critical safety question on German guns of this era and is not addressed.

analysis: A Winchester Model 12 shotgun engraved by Pauline Muerlle, $1,500-2,000. Muerlle is a documented and respected American firearms engraver, which makes this a named-maker object in a real sense -- the engraving, not the gun, is the art. Above the band at $1,980-2,640 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Modern firearm requiring transfer. The Model 12 itself is a common gun; the entire value is the engraving, and engraving attributions are asserted more often than documented. Look for the signature in the work.

analysis: A Beretta A400 Xtreme Unico 12-bore, $800-1,200. A current-production semi-automatic waterfowl gun. Above the band, modern, FFL transfer, no criteria fit.
problems: Above budget. Buying a current-production gun at 25% premium plus tax costs more than a dealer would charge.

analysis: A Marlin Golden 39-A with scope, .22 LR, $400-600. A well-regarded lever-action rimfire in continuous production; a shooter, not a collectable.
problems: Modern firearm, FFL transfer, no criteria fit. At $528-792 all-in you are paying dealer prices or more for a used rifle.

analysis: A Remington Model 12 rifle with scope, .22 LR, $1,500-2,000. The Model 12 pump .22 ran 1909-1936, so early examples straddle the antique line, and a scoped one in good condition is collectable. Above the band at $1,980-2,640 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Estimate is well above what a standard Model 12 makes -- $1,500-2,000 implies a special-order or high-condition example, and nothing in the title says which. Post-1899 in any case, so FFL transfer.

analysis: A sporterized Springfield 03-A3 in .30-06, $300-500. 'Sporterized' means a military rifle cut down and restocked for hunting -- which destroys the collector value of the original and leaves a serviceable deer rifle.
problems: Sporterizing is irreversible. Modern firearm, FFL transfer. No criteria fit. Estimate is roughly the market for a sporter, so there is no bargain either.
patience: Very high. Sporterized military rifles are everywhere.

analysis: A sporterized K98 in 8mm Mauser, $200-400. Same proposition as 1256: a wartime military action cut down for sporting use, with the collector value removed in the process.
problems: Sporterized, irreversible. Modern firearm, FFL transfer. Wartime German actions also carry markings that some buyers will not want on a wall.

analysis: A Winchester 1300 Hydro-Coil 12-bore, $300-500. A late-20th-century pump gun with a recoil-reducing stock. A shooter.
problems: Modern firearm, FFL transfer, no criteria fit. Estimate is above the used market for a 1300.

analysis: A Winchester 1300 youth 20-bore, $200-400. Companion to 1263. A used utility shotgun.
problems: Modern firearm, FFL transfer, no criteria fit. Estimate is at or above the used market.

analysis: A Neumann Freres side-by-side 12-bore, $300-500. Neumann Freres was a Liege trade name and the guns are competent Belgian production rather than best-gun work. Undated.
problems: No date, so the antique-firearm question is open. Belgian trade guns of this era very often have Damascus barrels, which cannot safely be fired with modern loads -- that is a safety issue, not just a value one, and the catalogue says nothing about barrel material or proof marks.
patience: Very high. Belgian trade doubles are extremely common and mostly unsaleable.

analysis: A prop lever action rifle, $200-400. Catalogued as a prop, so a non-functioning replica. Honest description, and it settles the matter.
problems: A replica with no age, no maker and no film provenance stated -- prop value comes entirely from documented production use, and none is claimed. Estimate assumes an association nobody has asserted.

analysis: A Sturmabteilung dagger, $500-700. Third Reich edged weapons have an active collecting market and the estimate reflects it. Post-1926, no criteria fit, and it is a category this analysis will simply note and move past.
problems: SA daggers are among the most extensively faked militaria in existence -- reproductions have been made since the 1950s and account for a large share of what is offered. No maker's mark, no RZM code, no condition information. Beyond authentication, this is a subject-matter decision the buyer should make on their own terms.

analysis: An Arabic dagger, $500-700 -- presumably a jambiya or khanjar. Undated, unattributed, no region named within a very large area.
problems: No date, no region, no materials. Arabian daggers are produced continuously for the tourist and gift trade and the older ones are hard to separate without handling. Note also that many carry rhinoceros-horn hilts, which would make them entirely unsaleable under CITES -- establish the hilt material before bidding. At $660-924 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band for something undated.

analysis: An identified Revolutionary War powder horn dated September 1775, Fort Ticonderoga, $10,000-15,000. A named, dated, place-identified horn from the first year of the Revolution is the top of American folk and military artefacts, and the estimate is a real market number. Ten to fifteen times the band.
problems: Massively above budget. At this level the inscription itself needs authenticating -- adding a name, a date and a fort to a genuine period horn is the classic enhancement, and Ticonderoga 1775 is the most desirable combination available, which is exactly why it is the most faked. Noted for completeness rather than as an opportunity.

analysis: A large Cape May, New Jersey Revolutionary War engraved powder horn, $1,000-1,500. Second of the three-horn consignment and the middle grade -- placed but apparently not dated. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Place-identified horns depend entirely on the inscription being period, and the same enhancement risk applies as at 2166. 'Rev War' is a dating inference. Consider 2168 instead, which is the same category inside the band.

analysis: A British powder horn dated 27 June 1795, from the French Revolutionary wars, $1,000-1,500. A specific inscribed date is the best evidence a horn can carry, and 1795 is comfortably antique. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Inscribed dates are also the most-added feature on powder horns; the test is whether the date cuts and patinates identically to the surrounding decoration. Fourth engraved horn in the sale, which is an unusual concentration and may mean one consignor -- worth asking about, because a single source for four scarce objects is itself information.

analysis: A J. Unertl 15X scope, $500-700 -- one of two identical Unertl lots (see 1251), part of an eight-lot vintage-riflescope consignment (1243, 1247, 1251, 1255, 1257, 1261, 1265 and the scoped rifles). Unertl target scopes are genuinely collected by benchrest and vintage-target shooters and hold their value well. Post-war, no criteria fit.
problems: Two identical Unertl 15X lots in one session compete directly. Vintage scope value depends on optical clarity, mount completeness and whether the original mounts and caps are present -- none stated. Post-1926.
patience: Very high -- there is a second one in this sale.

analysis: A J. Unertl 15X scope, $500-700 -- identical description to 1243, eight lots later. See that entry.
problems: Same as 1243, and competing with it.

analysis: A Lyman 30X Super Targetspot scope with case, $1,200-1,800 -- the highest-estimated scope in the consignment, and the 30X with its original case is the desirable configuration. Above the band at $1,584-2,376 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Post-1926. Optics of this age commonly have haze, fungus or separated cement, none of which shows in a photograph.

analysis: A Lyman All-American Perma Center 20X scope, $300-500 -- one of two identical lots (see 1265). Mid-century American target optics.
problems: Post-1926, no criteria fit. Two identical lots competing. Condition of the optics unstated.

analysis: A Lyman All-American Perma Center 20X scope, $300-500 -- identical to 1255. See that entry.
problems: Same as 1255.

analysis: A Lyman Super Targetspot 15X scope, $300-500. The lower-magnification sibling of 1247 and without a case.
problems: Post-1926, no criteria fit. Optical condition unstated.

analysis: A Leupold M8-4X scope, $200-400. A common and long-produced hunting scope; the cheapest and least collectable optic in the consignment.
problems: Post-1926, no criteria fit. Estimate is above the used market for an M8-4X.

analysis: Three Remington R1253 'Guide' bullet knives, $200-400 -- first of a four-lot Remington bullet-knife consignment (1245, 1252, 1259, 1262). Remington reintroduced the bullet knife in 1982 as an annual collectable and they were bought in quantity as an investment, which is why the secondary market is soft.
problems: 1980s-90s collectables sold as collectables, which is the worst possible provenance for future value. Boxed and unused examples are worth a modest premium and the catalogue does not say whether these are boxed. Post-1926, no criteria fit.
patience: Very high -- four lots of them in this sale alone.

analysis: Four Remington R4243 'Camp' bullet knives, $200-400. Second of the bullet-knife consignment; see 1245.
problems: Same as 1245.

analysis: Three Remington shotgun commemorative knives, $200-300. Third of the consignment and the least collected form -- commemorative knives are the bottom of the modern knife market.
problems: Same as 1245, and commemoratives are worse than the bullet knives.

analysis: Two Remington R1128 'Trapper' bullet knives, $200-300. Fourth and last of the bullet-knife consignment.
problems: Same as 1245. Two knives at $100-150 each is above the market.

analysis: A tooled leather buscadero gun belt and Brauer Bros. holster, $300-500. Brauer Brothers of St. Louis made holsters from the 1920s and the buscadero rig is the drop-loop Western style popularised by film. Attractive leatherwork, mid-century.
problems: Post-1926, no criteria fit. Leather rigs dry, crack and are frequently cut down; check the loop and stitching. Estimate is at the top of the market for a non-maker-marked rig, and Brauer is a maker but not a premium one.

analysis: Three Remington R1263 'Hunter' bullet knives, $100-200 -- the fifth and cheapest lot in the Remington bullet-knife consignment, and the only one where the estimate matches the market. See 1245 for the category.
problems: Same as 1245: 1980s-90s manufactured collectables with a soft secondary market. Post-1926, no criteria fit.
patience: Very high -- five lots of these in one sale.
